threads.thread_goal: Align on current issues and approve target workflow scope

messages.text: Kicking off the front-of-house workflow work for our Standardising Pharmacy Front-of-House Workflow and Stock Layout project_pack_ref: short project_title. For T1 we need to map what actually happens from when a customer walks in to when they leave with their medicines. I will start a draft in A1 capturing the current steps, but I need your input on pain points and safety risks. When you think about a typical shift at the counter: 1) Which parts feel messy or inconsistent between us 2) Where do you worry most about errors or missed checks 3) Which steps slow you down the most during busy times. Please reply with concrete examples from this week so we can agree what the new standard workflow must cover.

From the last few days, the handover between OTC questions and prescriptions is where I see confusion. Example: customer asks about a cough syrup, then hands over a script, and we sometimes start the OTC advice and forget to log the script in the system straight away. That creates a risk of the script being misplaced on the counter. Another point is when we receive repeats, we do not always check interactions with what they are buying OTC at the same time. For the new workflow, I think we need clear steps for: greeting and quick triage, separating scripts from OTC-only requests, and a visible place for scripts while we prepare them.

From my side, the main pain point is when we are juggling phone calls, walk-ins, and click-and-collect at the same time. I sometimes start checking a script, then get pulled to the phone, and when I come back I am not sure which step I was on. That is when I worry about missing a counselling point or a final check. Also, for OTC, we do not have a consistent way to document advice given for higher-risk products like emergency contraception. For the new workflow, could we include a simple prompt or tick box in A1 for when we must record advice, so it is not just in our heads.

From the shelves side, when I am helping at the front, I notice we lose time looking for products that are not where people expect them. Then the queue builds and we rush the handover. Maybe the workflow should say clearly who goes to the shelf and who stays at the counter, so we do not both leave the till. I am not sure how much of that belongs in A1 versus the layout map in A2, but I think the process should say how we ask for help from the shelf fillers during busy times.

One thing I struggle with is when customers bring back medicines for advice, like side effects or they say it is not working. Sometimes I am not sure if I should take them to the consultation area or just ask the pharmacist to come to the counter. It would help if the workflow in A1 had a simple rule for when to move to a more private space. Also, I get confused when we have to handle near-miss situations at the counter, like when we catch a wrong strength before handing it over. I do not always remember what to write down.

Adding a couple of points: 1) For new prescriptions, we are not consistent about confirming allergies and current medicines, especially when the customer is in a hurry. 2) For repeats, we sometimes skip checking storage advice and expiry dates on the label when handing over. I suggest the scope of the new workflow includes: intake and triage, safety checks before processing, counselling and handover, and a short step for documenting anything unusual, like near-miss or refusal of advice. That way T1 will give us a full picture from arrival to leaving.

Thanks all, this is helpful. I will update A1 with the current-state steps including: 1) customer arrival and quick triage, 2) script intake and safe parking spot, 3) OTC-only advice, 4) combined script plus OTC requests, 5) counselling and handover, 6) documentation of advice and near-miss. For T1 we also need to list pain points and safety risks. So far I have: scripts left on the counter, interruptions causing missed checks, inconsistent documentation of advice, unclear use of private space, and confusion about who leaves the till to fetch items. Please add anything I missed before we lock the scope.

Can we also include how we handle phone prescriptions and electronic scripts in the scope. Sometimes they get printed and mixed with paper scripts, and we do not have a clear place for them. That has caused delays and almost a mix-up once. I think that should be part of the standard process list too.

Agree with the list. For the private space question from 32339, maybe the workflow can say: if the discussion involves sensitive topics like sexual health, mental health, or visible distress, we offer the consultation area. We can keep it simple so new staff can follow it without needing to guess. That would also help with training later.

On who leaves the till, could we say that during peak hours the person logged into the till stays put, and the second person or shelf filler does the fetching. Outside peak times it can be more flexible. Not sure if that is too detailed for A1, but it would avoid both of us disappearing to the aisles.

That suggestion about the consultation area helps, thanks. Could we write it as a short rule in A1 so I can check it quickly when I am unsure. I sometimes hesitate because I do not want to make the customer uncomfortable by moving them if it is not needed.

Good point on electronic scripts. I suggest we add a specific step in the intake part of A1: confirm script source, print or tag it, and place it in the same designated script area as paper ones, with a small marker so we know it came electronically. That way T1 will reflect both paper and digital flows without creating a separate process.

I will capture that rule about who leaves the till as a simple line in the workflow, linked to our implementation schedule later in A8 so we can align with peak hours. Before we close this thread, we need to agree on which front-of-house processes are in scope and which pain points we tackle first. Based on the discussion, I propose the scope includes: 1) prescription intake and parking (paper and electronic), 2) OTC-only requests and combined script plus OTC, 3) counselling, handover, and documentation, 4) use of consultation area, 5) basic coordination with shelf fillers for fetching items. For top pain points, my suggestion is: a) scripts left on the counter or misplaced, b) interruptions leading to missed checks, c) inconsistent documentation of advice and near-miss. Please react or comment if you disagree.

Scope and top three pain points look right to me. The only small addition is to make sure we mention phone queries without scripts under OTC-only requests, but that is probably just wording in A1. I am happy to go ahead with that list.
I am aligned with that proposal. The three pain points you listed match what I see on late shifts. If we fix those, it should already reduce a lot of stress at the counter.
Works for me as well. I like that coordination with shelf fillers is included, even if it is just a couple of lines. That will help me know when I should step in.
I am ok with that list. Having the consultation area rule written down will help me a lot, so I am glad it is in scope.
Agree with both the scope and the three priority pain points. We can always refine smaller issues later once T1 is fully mapped.

Thanks all for confirming. To summarise and close this thread: we are agreeing that the front-of-house processes to standardise now are prescription intake and parking, OTC-only and combined requests, counselling and handover including documentation, use of consultation area, and basic coordination with shelf fillers. We are also agreeing that the first three pain points to address in the new workflow are scripts left on the counter or misplaced, interruptions leading to missed checks, and inconsistent documentation of advice and near-miss. I will mark these in A1 and complete T1 accordingly.

threads.thread_goal: Define and approve the standard shelf layout and labelling rules

messages.text: I have put together a first pass of the shelf layout map in A2 for the front-of-house medicines, linked to T2. It covers the main OTC categories and a small section for prescription-only items that are stored near the counter. I tried to group by condition (cough and cold, pain, stomach, skin, etc.) and keep high-risk medicines higher up and away from look-alikes. Before we move to T6 and pilot a section, can you look at the map and tell me: 1) does the flow make sense from a customer and safety point of view 2) are there any products you think must be moved for legal or counselling reasons 3) what would make it easier to find items quickly during busy times.

Thanks for sharing. Looking at A2, I like that cough and cold is near the front, but I am worried that some codeine-containing products are too close to standard painkillers. Could we separate those more clearly, maybe with a different shelf or at least a divider. Also, for emergency contraception and smoking cessation, I would prefer them closer to the consultation area so we can have a discreet conversation. That might mean swapping a couple of bays.

From a customer flow point of view, the condition-based grouping in A2 feels intuitive. One thing I noticed is that some skin products that require more counselling, like stronger steroid creams, are mixed with basic moisturisers. Could we either move them closer to the counter or add a clear label saying to ask at the counter. That would tie in with the labelling guideline in A3 and T4.

I sometimes get lost with the vitamins and supplements section. On the map in A2 it looks like they are spread across two bays. Would it be possible to keep them in one continuous run, maybe with sub-sections for general, pregnancy, and children. That would help me find things faster when the queue is long.

Agree with the points raised. From a safety angle, I would also suggest we clearly mark high-risk and temperature-sensitive items in both A2 and A3. For example, eye drops that need fridge storage after opening, or insulin pens that are kept in the fridge. Even if they are not all front-of-house, the layout and labelling rules should make it obvious where they live and how they are labelled, linking to T11.

I have reviewed A2 as well. Overall structure is good, but we need to be strict about separation of look-alike, sound-alike medicines and anything with higher misuse potential. For the labelling rules in A3 and T4, I propose we define: 1) a standard label colour or icon for high-risk items, 2) a rule that temperature-sensitive medicines have a clear storage icon and are not placed near heat sources, 3) a simple rule for where we place warning labels versus price labels. Once we agree on these, we can apply them in the pilot for T6.

Good catch on the codeine products. I can move them to a separate shelf behind the counter on the map in A2, with a front-of-house label saying to ask at the counter. For emergency contraception and smoking cessation, I will shift them closer to the consultation area as you suggested. I will update the map and share a quick screenshot in the channel later today.

On the skin products, I am not fully sure which ones need more counselling. Could one of you mark them in A2 or list them in a comment on A3 so I can group them near the counter or add a label saying to speak to us. I do not want to move the wrong ones.

Sure, I can go through the skin section and mark the products that usually require more counselling directly in A2 later today. For A3, I will also suggest a short rule like: if the product has steroid, strong acid, or is for intimate areas, we add a small label saying to ask at the counter. That should keep it simple.
If vitamins are in one run with clear sub-sections, that will really help me. Could we also have shelf labels that say adults, pregnancy, children, so I do not have to read every box when it is busy.

I like the idea of icons for high-risk and temperature-sensitive items. For T11 we are already listing temperature-sensitive medicines, so we can reuse that list in A3. Maybe we can define that high-risk items get a red triangle icon on the shelf label, and temperature-sensitive get a blue snowflake. That should be easy to spot during daily checks and when training new staff.

For the labelling rules, can we also include font size and where we place the label on the shelf edge. Sometimes price labels cover important information. If A3 says, for example, that safety icons are always on the left and price on the right, it will be easier to keep it consistent.

Yes, we should be specific. I will draft in A3 that shelf labels must have minimum font size for medicine names, safety icons on the left, price on the right, and no overlapping of safety information. For high-risk and temperature-sensitive items, we will add the red triangle and blue snowflake icons as suggested. Once that is in, we can test it in the pilot section for T6.

I have now updated A2 with: 1) codeine products moved behind the counter, 2) emergency contraception and smoking cessation closer to the consultation area, 3) vitamins in one continuous run with sub-sections, 4) a note to align skin products with the counselling list that 20729 will mark. Unless there are strong objections, I suggest we use this updated map as the initial standard layout for the cough and cold plus vitamins section in T6.

Updated layout sounds good to me. Using cough and cold plus vitamins as the pilot area for T6 makes sense, since that is where we spend a lot of time. I am comfortable calling this our initial standard layout for that section.

I am happy with the updated A2 as well. The separation of codeine and the move of sensitive products closer to the consultation area address my main concerns. Ok to proceed with this as the initial standard for the pilot.
The vitamins layout looks much clearer now. I am fine with using this version for the pilot.

The labelling rules you described in A3 cover what I need for daily work and checks. As long as high-risk and temperature-sensitive icons are standard, it will be easier to spot issues quickly. I am ok to adopt these rules for the pilot section.

To close this out: we seem aligned that the updated A2 layout for cough and cold plus vitamins will be our initial standard for the pilot in T6, and that the labelling rules in A3 will include: condition-based grouping, separation of codeine and other higher-risk items, icons for high-risk and temperature-sensitive medicines, and fixed positions for safety icons and prices. I will record this as our agreed starting point and we can refine after the pilot feedback.

threads.thread_goal: Lock in SOPs for stock reception and daily checks

messages.text: I have drafted the steps for receiving and storing new stock in A1, linked to T3, and a first version of the daily shelf and stock verification checklist in A5 for T9. For stock reception, the draft covers: delivery arrival, checking items against the order, checking storage conditions and expiry dates, documenting discrepancies, and placing items either in the dispensary or front-of-house according to A2 and A3. For the daily checklist, it includes stock levels, expiry checks, and label accuracy per aisle. Before we finalise, can you review and tell me: 1) if any steps are missing or unclear, 2) if the daily checklist is realistic for a normal shift, and 3) if there are any legal or organisational checks we should add.

Looking at the stock reception part in A1, I like that you included expiry checks and discrepancy documentation. One thing I am not sure about is where we record temperature checks for deliveries that should be kept cold. Should that be part of this SOP or in a separate fridge log. Also, for T3, maybe we should add a step to separate short-dated items so we can place them in a more visible spot for rotation.

On the daily checklist in A5 for T9, the structure is clear, but I am a bit worried about the time it might take. For example, checking every expiry date in a long aisle every day might not be realistic. Could we define that we check all high-risk and temperature-sensitive items daily, and the rest on a rotating schedule, like one aisle per day. That way we still meet safety expectations without overloading the shift.

From the shelf filler side, A5 looks doable if we adjust the time estimates. Right now it says 10 minutes per aisle, but in reality some aisles take longer. Maybe we can add a column for small, medium, large aisles with different time estimates. Also, could we include a quick check that shelf labels match the layout in A2, so we catch any drift early.

I am a bit confused about when exactly we should document discrepancies. In A1 it says to record them, but not where. Do we use the same incident log as near-miss in A7, or is there a separate stock discrepancy form. I do not want to put it in the wrong place.

Good question. For stock discrepancies that are not safety incidents, we usually use the stock adjustment form in our system, and only use A7 when there is a near-miss or incident that could affect a patient. I suggest we clarify in A1 that T3 requires us to: 1) record quantity or product mismatches in the stock system, and 2) log any safety-related issues, like wrong medicine delivered, in A7 as a near-miss.

On temperature checks, I will add to A1 that for deliveries of temperature-sensitive medicines we: 1) check the delivery temperature on arrival, 2) record it in the fridge or temperature log, and 3) if out of range, quarantine and inform the pharmacist. For short-dated items, I will add a step to mark them and place them in a designated area for faster rotation, aligned with T11.

For A5, I agree we need to balance safety and time. I will adjust T9 so that: 1) high-risk and temperature-sensitive items are checked daily, 2) other items are checked on a rotating basis, one aisle per day, and 3) we include a quick visual scan for obvious issues in all aisles. I will also add a field to capture the actual time taken per aisle during the first week so we can refine the estimates.

The rotating schedule and time capture in A5 sound good. That will help us see what is realistic. Could we also add a simple tick box for when shelf labels do not match A2, so we can flag it without writing long notes.

For the reception SOP in A1, one more thing: can we include a step to separate medicines that need extra security, like controlled drugs, and make it clear that we do not leave them unattended on the bench. Even if the detailed controlled drugs process is elsewhere, a reminder here would help.
Thanks, that makes it clearer. If A1 says when to use the stock system and when to use A7, I will be more confident I am recording things in the right place.

On the daily checklist, could we add a quick check that medicines that should not be in front-of-house, like certain prescription-only items, have not drifted onto the OTC shelves. Maybe a line in A5 that says to confirm that restricted items are only where they should be according to A2.

I will update A5 to include: 1) a tick box for label mismatch with A2, 2) a line to confirm no restricted items have drifted to front-of-house, and 3) the rotating expiry check schedule. Once that is done, T9 should meet the definition of done, and we can test it for a week and refine.

I will also add to A1 that on receipt we immediately separate controlled and other high-security medicines, place them in the secure area, and follow the separate controlled drugs SOP. That way T3 stays aligned with our legal obligations without duplicating the full procedure.

From a compliance point of view, the updated A1 now covers deliveries, storage conditions, expiry checks, discrepancy documentation, temperature checks, and security-sensitive items. That matches what I would expect for T3. I am comfortable saying the SOP is complete from our side, pending pharmacist review.
The revised A5 sounds workable. With the rotating schedule and time tracking, I think we can manage it on normal shifts. I am ok to use this checklist format for the trial week in T9.

Agreed. The reception SOP in A1 now reads clearly enough that new staff could follow it with minimal help. I support moving forward with this version and sending it to the pharmacist for a quick compliance check.
I am also fine with the A5 format. The daily focus on high-risk and temperature-sensitive items plus rotating other aisles feels like the right balance.
With the clarifications in A1 and A5, I feel more confident about what to do when I find an issue. I am ok to start using these documents once they are final.

To wrap up this thread: we have an agreed SOP in A1 for receiving and storing new stock that covers deliveries, storage conditions, expiry checks, discrepancy documentation, temperature-sensitive items, and security-sensitive medicines, aligned with T3. We also have an agreed daily shelf and stock verification checklist format in A5 for T9, with daily checks for high-risk and temperature-sensitive items, rotating checks for other aisles, label and layout verification against A2, and time tracking for refinement. I will send A1 and A5 to the pharmacist for a quick review, but from our side we can treat these as our standard documents.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on training approach and rollout schedule

messages.text: Now that the main workflows and layout pieces are drafted, we need to agree how we train everyone and when we roll out changes without affecting peak hours. I have started a training checklist in A4 for T5 that covers: new front-of-house workflow in A1, shelf layout in A2, labelling rules in A3, customer communication guide in A6, and daily checklist in A5. I also added a first pass of an implementation schedule in A8 for T10, based on our usual busy times. Proposal: 1) short, 20-minute huddles at the start of shifts using A6 and A1, 2) a sign-off in A4 for each topic per person, and 3) layout changes done in off-peak slots from A8. Please share if this format works for you and if the schedule matches your experience of busy periods.

Looking at A4, the checklist topics make sense. For the format, I think short huddles are good, but we might also need a quick one-page summary for people who miss a session, especially for customer communication in A6. Maybe T7 can give us a laminated sheet at the counter that we can refer to and tick off in A4 once we have gone through it.

On the schedule in A8 for T10, the peak hours you listed mostly match what I see, but Saturday late morning is busier than the sheet suggests. I would avoid doing any layout changes then. Also, for training, I learn better by doing, so could we include a short role-play using A6 during the huddles, not just reading through it.

For shelf fillers, the training in A4 that matters most is A2, A3, and A5. Could we have a separate section in A4 just for shelf fillers, so we do not have to sign off on things we are not responsible for. Also, in A8, please make sure the layout change slots do not clash with our usual delivery unpacking times, or we will be stretched.

I sometimes struggle to remember everything from a single huddle. Would it be possible to have a simple checklist at the counter, maybe from A6 and A1, that I can glance at during the shift. That would help me feel more confident when answering questions.

For T5, I suggest we define in A4 who must complete which parts: all assistants complete workflow, communication, and near-miss sections; shelf fillers complete layout, labelling, and daily checklist sections; and everyone signs off on basic safety points. For T10, I agree with avoiding Saturday late morning and also weekday 5-7pm. We can use A8 to block those times and only schedule changes in quieter slots.

Good idea on the one-page summary. T7 is already about a quick-reference guide, so I will make sure A6 is formatted to fit on one page and we can laminate a couple of copies for the counter and consultation area. I will also add a field in A4 to confirm that each person has reviewed the quick-reference guide, even if they missed the live huddle.

On A8, I will adjust Saturday to mark late morning as peak and block it for changes. For training, we can definitely include a short role-play in each huddle using A6, for example practising how to handle a sensitive query or explain waiting times while we follow the new workflow in A1.

I will split A4 into sections: one for all staff, one for assistants, and one for shelf fillers, and note in T5 who needs to complete which. In A8, I will also overlay delivery times so we do not schedule layout changes during heavy unpacking. We can use the quieter mid-morning or mid-afternoon slots instead.
The way you split responsibilities in A4 makes sense to me. It is clearer than everyone signing everything. For the training format, I am happy with short huddles plus the laminated A6 sheet.
Role-play plus the quick-reference in A6 will work well for me. As long as A8 keeps changes away from Saturday late morning and weekday evenings, I am comfortable with the schedule.

Thanks for separating the sections in A4. For shelf fillers, I confirm we can attend one huddle focused on A2, A3, and A5, and then sign off in our part of the checklist. The off-peak slots you mentioned in A8 sound fine as long as we keep them flexible if deliveries are delayed.
I like the idea of a simple checklist at the counter. If A6 and A1 can be summarised into a few key prompts, that will help me remember the steps when it is busy.

From my side, I support the training format you proposed: short shift huddles, role-play using A6, laminated quick-reference, and sign-off in A4. For T10, I will help refine A8 with the store manager to confirm peak and off-peak times and then share the final schedule here.

To summarise what we have so far: 1) Training will be delivered via short start-of-shift huddles with role-play using A6 and A1, plus laminated one-page guides at the counter and consultation area. 2) A4 will track completion by topic, with separate sections for all staff, assistants, and shelf fillers, and everyone will sign off on the parts relevant to their role. 3) The implementation schedule in A8 for T10 will avoid Saturday late morning, weekday 5-7pm, and heavy delivery times, focusing layout changes in quieter mid-morning and mid-afternoon slots. If anyone disagrees with this approach, please say so; otherwise I will treat this as our agreed training format and schedule outline and take A8 to the store manager for confirmation.
I am happy with that summary. The format and schedule work for me.
Aligned from my side as well.
Works for shelf fillers too.
I am ok with this plan.
All good from me. I will coordinate with the store manager on A8 and confirm the final schedule.

Great, thanks everyone. I will mark in A4 that our agreed training format is short shift huddles with role-play plus laminated quick-reference guides, and that all assistants and shelf fillers must complete the relevant sections. I will also update A8 with the agreed off-peak slots and work with 255566 and the store manager to finalise the schedule for T10. Once confirmed, we will share the final version here and start booking sessions.

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results, near-miss logs, and finalise follow-ups

messages.text: We have now run the pilot layout in the cough and cold plus vitamins section for a week under T6, and logged any near-miss or issues in A7. I have also drafted a short summary of outcomes and follow-up actions in T12, referencing the updated workflow in A1 and layout in A2. Overall, picking times improved and we had fewer interruptions, but there were a couple of near-miss entries related to similar packaging and one case of a product being shelved in the wrong sub-section. I would like to hear from each of you: 1) what worked well in the pilot, 2) what did not work or felt confusing, and 3) any changes you think we must make before rolling this out to the rest of the store.

From my shifts, the new layout in A2 made it easier to find cough and cold products, and the separation of codeine items worked well. I noticed fewer customers waiting while I searched. One issue I saw, which is in A7, was a near-miss where a non-drowsy and drowsy product with similar packaging were next to each other and almost swapped. Maybe we should add a clearer shelf label or a small divider between them.

I agree that picking felt smoother. The vitamins sub-sections in A2 helped a lot. One thing that did not work so well was that some customers still went straight to the stronger cough syrups without speaking to us, even though we moved them. Maybe we need more prominent signage or a label from A3 saying to ask at the counter for certain products. Also, I found the near-miss log in A7 easy to use once I got used to it.

From the shelf side, the daily checks using A5 in the pilot area were manageable. I did log one issue in A7 where a vitamin product ended up in the wrong age sub-section, probably during a busy time. It was easy to spot because of the new labels, but maybe we should add a quick reminder in the training to double-check age group before shelving.

I liked having the condition-based layout. It made it easier for me to help customers find things. I did get confused once about where to put a combination cold and flu product that could fit in two places. I was not sure which sub-section in A2 it belonged to. Maybe we can add a small rule or example list for those borderline products.

Looking at the entries in A7 and the draft summary in T12, the main themes I see are: 1) improved speed and fewer interruptions, 2) a couple of near-miss cases due to similar packaging, and 3) minor mis-shelving in the vitamins section. I suggest we update A3 to strengthen the labelling rules for look-alike products, for example using more distinct icons or spacing, and add a short note in A1 about how to handle borderline products like combination cold and flu items.

On the drowsy versus non-drowsy near-miss in A7, I agree we should separate them more clearly. I will update A2 to place them on different shelves or at least with a divider, and A3 to require a clear label indicating drowsy or non-drowsy on the shelf edge. That should reduce the chance of confusion.

For the stronger cough syrups, we can add a more prominent sign based on A3, for example a label saying speak to us before choosing this product. We can also mention this in the customer communication guide in A6 so we remember to prompt customers when we see them looking at that shelf.

I can add a small reminder in the shelf filler section of A4 to double-check age group when shelving vitamins, and maybe a short note in A5 to glance at the age label when doing checks. That should help avoid mis-shelving.

For combination cold and flu products, maybe we can agree a simple rule in A1 and A2, like placing them in a specific sub-section called combination relief, and adding a note in A3 that they should always be there. That way we are consistent.
A combination relief sub-section would help me a lot. If A2 shows it clearly and A3 mentions it, I will know where to put those products.

On the workflow side in A1, I noticed that with the new layout I had more time to follow the standard counselling steps, and the quick-reference in A6 helped with consistent messages. I did not see any new risks introduced by the pilot, as long as we implement the extra labelling changes we discussed.

For T12, I can help refine the summary to highlight the benefits we saw, like reduced picking time and fewer interruptions, and list the specific follow-up actions: update A2 and A3 for look-alike products and combination relief, adjust A4 and A5 for age-group reminders, and keep using A7 for ongoing near-miss monitoring.
Once you update A2 and A3, I can re-label the shelves in the pilot area and take new photos for T6, so we have a clear before and after record.
I will also add a short example in A6 on how to approach customers looking at the stronger cough syrups, so we are consistent in how we start that conversation.
The daily checks in A5 were a bit new to me at first, but after a couple of days they became routine. I think keeping them in place will help catch mis-shelving early.
I agree with the proposed changes. Once we separate drowsy and non-drowsy more clearly and add the combination relief sub-section, I think we can safely roll this layout out to similar sections.

Thanks for all the feedback. I will update T12 to capture: 1) key benefits from the pilot, 2) the near-miss themes from A7, and 3) the agreed follow-up actions on A2, A3, A4, A5, and A6. After that, we can share the summary with the pharmacist and store manager and propose rolling the layout and processes out to the remaining sections in phases, continuing to log any near-miss in A7.
